37	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
38	
39	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
40	
41	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
42	- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
43	- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
44	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
45	- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised, or a static error of a phase before the run, such as the disambiguator's, counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test here records a refusal that walk misses: it is green while the program loads and runs clean, and red once walk refuses it.
46	
47	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:
48	
49	- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
50	- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
51	- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
52	- `one_library_tests/`: a test whose program compiles against the one library: a test of a binding of the one library, or of a defect that only that library shows. Its tests compile with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, and `ant testOneLibrary` and `testFast` run them. A plain run test there runs against the one library's jars, as `OneLibraryRunHello.test` does. `compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet", lists what it cannot run, and `tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests", says how to run it.
53	- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series. Put no new test there.
54	
55	The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
56	
57	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
58	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
59	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
60	    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
61	                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
62	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
63	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
64	
65	A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. With `run_exits_nonzero=true`, the run must exit non-zero, as a program whose class fails to load does. The `run_*` checks, and the `PASS` check where no `run_out` check is given, still apply. For example:
66	
67	    tests=EqualityRung1
68	    link
69	    run
70	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS

83	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

For one thread, run the program directly with the prefix `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (a compiled program: `compiler.md`, "Running"), and check its exit code and output.

1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the five JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs its tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 11 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
20	- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.
21	
22	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs its tests in four shards, in a few minutes.
23	
24	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
25	
26	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
27	
28	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
29	
30	The two suites work in the same way:
31	
32	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
33	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
34	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
35	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
36	
37	To run a suite:
38	
39	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
40	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
41	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
42	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
43	
44	## The switches that the harness reads
45	
46	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
47	
48	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
49	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
51	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
52	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
53	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
54	
55	## Outside the gate
56	
57	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
58	- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
59	  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
60	  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
61	  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
62	  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
63	  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
64	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
65	
66	## When to run a whole suite
67	
68	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
69	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
70	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
71	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
72	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
73	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
74	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
75	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
76	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests. After an edit of one of the fourteen components that `OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles, also run `ant testOneLibrary` (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
77	
78	The suites do not check these:
79	
80	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
81	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
82	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
83	- `fortress unparse`;
84	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
85	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
86	
87	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
88	
89	## One test, or a few
90	
91	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
92	
93	### Interpreter tests
94	
95	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
96	
97	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
98	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
99	
100	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
101	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
102	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
103	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
104	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
105	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
106	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
107	
108	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
109	
110	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
111	
112	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
113	
114	### Compiled tests
115	
116	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library, and a run test there needs the jars of its fourteen components. Run the tests in one of these ways:
117	
118	- `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, with `OneLibraryComponents.test`, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. Each suite deletes that folder when it starts, and only `testFast` and `testOneLibrary` fill it again.
119	- With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first. The compiles write to `default_repository/caches-one`, and the jars stay there after the call. Its `FortressLibrary` alone takes about 135 to 160 s, so run the call in the background (`session.md`).
120	- For a run by hand against the onelibrary track's jars, set `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary` and `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. The build does not touch that folder, so run `ant testOneLibrary` again after an edit of Java or Scala.
121	
122	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
123	
124	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
125	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
126	
127	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
128	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
129	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
130	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
131	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
132	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
133	
134	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
135	
136	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
137	
138	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.
139	
140	## One unit-test class, or one track

142	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
143	
144	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:
145	
146	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
147	- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
148	- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
149	- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
150	- `ant testOneLibrary`: the onelibrary track.

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
13	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
14	- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
15	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
16	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
17	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
18	
19	## How to commit
20	
21	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
22	
23	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
24	
25	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
26	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
27	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
28	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
29	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
30	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
31	
32	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
33	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
34	
35	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
36	
37	## Pushing
38	
39	Push after every commit.
40	
41	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
42	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree leaves its branch. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
43	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
44	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
45	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
46	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
47	
48	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The platform rebuilds a lost container from `blinded-fable`.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
53

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59

== Specification/basic/expressions/bindings.tex:12-121

\section{Assignments}
\seclabel{assignment}

\note{Qualified names are not yet supported.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{AssignExpr}
&::=& \emph{AssignLefts} \emph{AssignOp} \emph{Expr}\\

\emph{AssignLefts}
&::=& \texttt( \emph{AssignLeft}(\EXP{,} \emph{AssignLeft})$^*$ \texttt)\\
&$|$& \emph{AssignLeft}\\

\emph{AssignLeft}
&::=& \emph{SubscriptExpr}\\
&$|$& \emph{FieldSelection}\\
&$|$& \emph{QualifiedName}\\

\emph{SubscriptExpr} &::=&
\emph{Primary} \emph{LeftEncloser} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}} \option{\emph{ExprList}} \emph{RightEncloser} \\

\emph{FieldSelection} &::=& \emph{Primary}\EXP{.}\emph{Id}\\

\emph{AssignOp} &::=& \EXP{\ASSIGN} $|$ (\emph{Encloser} $|$ \emph{Op})\EXP{=}

\end{Grammar}

An assignment expression consists of a left-hand side
(\emph{AssignLefts}) indicating one or more variables, subscripted
expressions (as described in \secref{subscripted-assignment}), or
field accesses to be updated, an assignment token, and a
right-hand-side expression.  Multiple left-hand sides must be grouped
using tuple notation (comma-separated and parenthesized).  Variables
updated in an assignment expression must already be declared.

The assignment token `\EXP{\ASSIGN}' indicates ordinary assignment.
Ordinary assignment proceeds in two phases.  In the first, the evaluation phase, the
right-hand-side expression is evaluated in parallel with each of the
left-hand-side subexpressions, forming an implicit thread group.
Evaluating a left-hand variable does nothing.  Evaluating a left-hand
field reference evaluates the receiving object.  Evaluating a
left-hand subscripting operation evaluates the receiving object and
the index in parallel in a nested thread group.  After the outer
implicit thread group completes normally, the assignment phase begins.  Each component of the right-hand-side value is
assigned to the corresponding component of the left-hand side in
parallel, forming an implicit thread group.  Assigning a left-hand
variable simply changes the binding for the variable's location to
contain the new value.
Assigning a left-hand field reference calls
the corresponding setter method on the reiver object, passing the new value.
Assigning a left-hand subscript simply calls the subscripted
assignment operation on the corresponding object with the new value.

Any operator (other than `\EXP{\COLONOP}' or `\EXP{=}' or `\EXP{<}' or
`\EXP{>}') followed by `\EXP{=}' with no intervening whitespace
indicates compound (updating) assignment.  This adds an additional
phase to assignment between the two phases of ordinary assignment.
In the first phase, a
left-hand field reference invokes the getter for
the corresponding field after the receiving object has been evaluated.
A left-hand subscripting operation invokes the subscripting operator
on the receiving object once receiver and index have been evaluated.  A
left-hand variable simply returns the current value of the location
associated with that variable.  In the new second phase, the operator
indicated in the assignment is invoked.  The left-hand argument is the
value of the left-hand expression evaluated in the first phase; the
right-hand argument is the value evaluated for the right-hand side of
the assignment expression.  When the operator evaluation completes
normally, the assignment phase is run as in ordinary assignment.

The important point to understand is that compound assignment evaluates
its subexpressions exactly once, and that the parts of assignment
proceed implicitly in parallel where possible.
The value and type of an assignment expression is \EXP{()}.
The type of the right-hand side must be a subtype of the type of the left-hand
side.

Consider the following assignment:
%(a[i], b.x, c) += f(t,u,v)
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.Assign.a.tex}
Here in the first phase we evaluate \VAR{a} and \VAR{i} in parallel,
then when this completes we invoke the indexing method of
\VAR{a} to evaluate \EXP{a_i}.
In parallel, we evaluate \VAR{b} and then
call the getter method \EXP{b.x}.
In parallel, we look up the value of variable \VAR{c}.
Finally, we evaluate \EXP{f(t,u,v)} in parallel with all of
these left-hand sides.
In the second phase, we combine the results using the \EXP{+} operator,
to evaluate \EXP{(a_i,b.x,c) \mathrel{+} f(t,u,v)}.
This must return a tuple of three values \EXP{(p,q,r)}.
In the final phase, in parallel we
call the indexed assignment operator \EXP{a_i \ASSIGN p},
call the setter \EXP{b.x\ASSIGN{}q},
and perform the local assignment
\EXP{c\ASSIGN{}r}.

Here are some simpler and more commonplace examples of assignment:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.Assign.b.tex}

\subsection{Definite Assignment}
\seclabel{definite-assignment}

\note{Definite assignment check is not supported yet.}

References to uninitialized variables are statically forbidden. As with the
Java Programming Language, this static constraint is ensured with a specific
conservative flow analysis. In essence, an initialization of a variable
must occur on every possible execution path to each reference to a
variable.

A trait declaration contains a set of method declarations.
Syntactically, a method declaration begins with
an optional sequence of modifiers followed by
the method's name,
optional static parameters
(described in \chapref{trait-parameters}),
the value parameter with its (optionally) declared type,
an optional type of a return value,
an optional declaration of thrown checked exceptions
(discussed in \chapref{exceptions}),
an optional \KWD{where} clause
(discussed in \secref{where-clauses}),
a contract for the method (discussed in \secref{method-contracts}),
and finally an optional body expression preceded by the token \EXP{=}.
If a method declaration has the \KWD{getter} modifier,
it does not affect the behavior of a program; rather,
it documents that the method is intended to serve as a getter.
A \KWD{throws} clause does not include naked type variables.
Every element in a \KWD{throws} clause is a subtype of
\TYP{CheckedException}.


Method declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{getter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{getter} explicitly declares a
getter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field declaration.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit getter for the field.
An explicitly declared getter method must take no arguments and return a
result of the field's type.
A getter method must not throw any checked exception.
Getter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A getter method must be invoked with the field access syntax:
%expr.id
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{expr}.\VAR{id}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{id} is the name of the getter method.



\paragraph{\KWD{setter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{setter} explicitly declares a
setter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit setter for the field.
An explicitly declared setter method must take a single argument---the
value being set---and return \EXP{()}.
A setter method must not throw any checked exception.
Setter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A setter method must be invoked with the \emph{assignment syntax}:
%expr1.id := expr2
\begin{Fortress}
\({expr}_{1}.\VAR{id} \ASSIGN {expr}_{2}\)
\end{Fortress}


We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.




There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\revision{revival-self-type}{In a trait \VAR{T} with a self-type parameter \VAR{X}
(\secref{trait-decls}), this remains the type of the \KWD{self} parameter
in the declaration's signature, which overloading and the choice of a declaration
at a call read, save the test of whether two overloaded declarations' parameter
types exclude each other, which reads it as \EXP{T \cap X}; in the method's body
\KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X} (\secref{idn-ref}).}
Semantically, functional method declarations can be viewed as top-level
function declarations.  For example, the following overloaded functional method
\VAR{f} declared within a trait declaration \VAR{A}:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.a.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.b.tex}
may be rewritten as top-level functions as follows:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.c.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.d.tex}
where \VAR{internalF} is a freshly generated name.
Functional method declarations may be overloaded with top-level function
declarations.
An abstract function declaration
(described in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations})
can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations.
See \chapref{multiple-dispatch} for a discussion of overloaded
functionals in Fortress.

When a method declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{method definition}.
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method: a method definition with the same name and the self parameter (if any)
at the same position whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self
parameter, is that of the abstract method declaration, or definitions whose
parameter types are subtypes of it and together cover it
(\secref{internal-types}), or it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said only that
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.
The object defines the method by a body at its parameter type, or by bodies at
narrower parameter types that together cover it, \KWD{comprises} clauses read
at the level of values (\secref{trait-decls}), as
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks of the concrete declarations for an
abstract function declaration; one body at a narrower parameter type that does
not cover the abstract method's does not define it.
This is the rule of the type group's compiled type checker (2012) and of its
calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012).
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged: it defines them in this
sense.}
An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter
types cannot be omitted except for the self parameter.


\note{
Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not
accessible.  They are not considered for overloading checks.

Partial overriding of an overloaded functional is allowed
but partial overriding of a functional declaration is not allowed.
}

A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.
Such a declaration \emph{overrides} any inherited declaration with the same name
and the self parameter (if any) at the same position,
whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter,
is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type.
The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of
that of the overridden declaration to preserve type safety.
A declaration with the modifier \KWD{override} must override
some inherited declaration.
It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier \KWD{override}
does not override any inherited declaration.

## Deviations from the ruling

1. Step 1 expected the `VerifyError` from a one-JVM compile in the way `tests-running.md:119` gives. That run, and the same under the hash flag, compiled `QQ`'s calls at `QQ` and ran 'Hello, one library'; the failure reproduced only in ant's onelibrary JVM (the runs above). Row 1100 had recorded the same: `Ratio` "when `FortressLibrary` compiles after other programs in one JVM", `QQ` "compiled first in a fresh JVM".
2. Step 3's test did not flip either build by the flag. Its condition for step 4 held all the same, the merged code under the flag making the base's call, and the one build disagreed with itself between JVMs, which no rung's logic can do; so step 3's bisect did not run.
3. Step 4's premise, that `Ratio`'s declaration is not applicable at the arguments' static types, is wrong against the specification: in a trait with a `comprises` clause `self` has the type `T ∩ (U1 ∪ … ∪ Un)` (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:63-69`), so `Ratio`'s `denominator(self)` is applicable at `self`'s static type. With `QQ`'s declaration at `QQ` (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:609`), the specification's static choice is the more specific, `Ratio`'s (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:355-358`). The checker reads `QQ`'s own `self` parameter as the same meet, so it ties the two, and no iteration picks between them by a rule. The repair makes the tie's choice free of the order as "The repair" says. The call's static type at such a tie is the head's return type, `QQ`'s; where a listed type's declaration returns a strictly narrower type, the specification gives the narrower. No such pair is in either library's tie sites (all 38 are `ZZ`).
4. Step 6 asked the test to assert the value of the getter that calls `f(self)`. Running that getter dies, after the fix, with row 815's missing overload method: the call names the overloading of the trait's and the object's declarations, `\=f{...}`, which the component's class does not hold. A scratch copy of the test that asserts `s.total`, `SelfGetterValueProbe`, compiled and run on the fixed tree with a private copy of the prelude's caches (`bin/fortress compile SelfGetterValueProbe.fss`, then `bin/fortress run SelfGetterValueProbe`): 'java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'com.sun.fortress.compiler.runtimeValues.FZZ32 SelfGetterValueProbe.\=width{_|tmp|repair-gate|probe|SelfGetterValueProbe\,fss\!15\!5-25,_|tmp|repair-gate|probe|SelfGetterValueProbe\,fss\!8\!5-21}(SelfGetterValueProbe$Solid)''. The same died so on the merged code before the fix in the default hash mode, where every call took `Solid`'s arrow. So the test asserts what the repair fixes, that the default methods verify and load, through the second getter; the getter's value waits for row 815 (climb batch 35's run 2, fork M2). The one library's `QQ` methods that call `numerator` or `denominator` on `self` are in the same state as on the base: they load, and a call of one would meet row 815.
5. Step 8 asked to add to row 996 the site and the test, or to open a row if the site is not the code generator's. The site is the checker's, and row 1100, opened by climb batch 34b's rung C, already records this failure, so no row was opened: row 1100 was rewritten as traced (its claim said the dispatch method took `Ratio`; it is the call's arrow), with this test as its reproducer, and row 996 got a note naming row 1100. Row 1100 closes once the commit is on `main`: `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py close 1100 --commit <hash> --test ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall`, a step after the commit, which the one-commit rule of this stage leaves to the next.

13:The batch's generator writes each run's manifest from this section. Each rung's `section` is its section 4 heading, word for word without its backticks. Run 1, climb batch 35, holds R, W, S, O and A in that order; run 2, climb batch 35b, holds E, L and M. No two rungs of a run are expected to edit one file; where a rung may reach a file that another names, section 4, "The rule the rungs keep", gives each its members. The expected minutes order the scatter only. REC stands for `doc:explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-35.md#`, PRB for `doc:explorations/compile-ladder/plan-35/probes/fixes-35.md#`, SPEC for `doc:Specification/`, and SRC for `code:ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`. A briefing key marked (check) is also in the rung's `checks` list, which its skeptic, a judge and a repair round read. Every key was checked with `facts-extract.sh --check` on `main`, each of the 67 distinct keys matching one place, REC's on this record as committed.
52:  - PRB `1. Under walk, on the base` (check): the walk test's failure on the base.
77:  - PRB `1. Under walk, on the base` (check): both failures on the base.

443:Two effects that come near microGPT, neither consequential by the rule: fork W2 makes the model's top-level constants run once under walk, at load, with the same values and no line changed; fork E1 adds an operator that no component of the model declares or uses, and the quick pair passed with it (PRB section 4).
450:2. **B2. What the batch takes.** The fixes of section 1, chosen from the inventory's group (a) where the two paths differ or depart from the specification, a program meets the defect, and the fix is small. **Default: so.** Rows 964, 963 and 1044 move to the forks that wait (section 2): each needs an answer first (PRB section 5). Row 1017 stays in group (a) for a later batch: its fix reaches every numeral at a generic declaration, and needs a count first. A program that writes any of these meets today's behaviour.

57	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do

60	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
61	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
62	        echo "# atomic $p run$i threads=4 $r"
63	      done
64	    done

66	The gate is red on any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE.
67	
68	## The ladder regression
69	
70	The compile ladder records how far each test program gets through the compiler's phases, in order: parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run and pass. The ladder regression runs part of it again, and compares the result with the baseline, `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/`:
71	
72	- It compiles and runs the 85 programs of the baseline's `pass-list.txt`. It compares each one's phase and output with the baseline's `raw/`.
73	- It compiles the eighteen components of the two microGPT programs, and never runs them. It compares each one's phase with the baseline's `microgpt-phase.md`.
74	
75	A file that moved gets a mark:
76	
77	- DOWN: a phase lower than the record.
78	- MISSING: a file with no output.
79	- STDOUT: output that differs from the record after the `Operation took <n>ms` line is masked.
80	- UP: a phase higher than the record. This is progress, not red.
81	
82	DOWN, MISSING and STDOUT are red, unless your brief declared that move as expected before the gate ran.
83	Warning: do not run `run-ladder.sh`, the driver over every test program, with its defaults. Its default root is shared, its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run, and its default `OUT` is a tracked folder.
84	
85	To run it, as step 7, with step 3's copies of the caches:
86	
87	1. Copy the drivers into `tmp/gate/ladder/`, and point their outputs and caches there:
88	
89	       D=$PWD/tmp/gate/ladder ; B=explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19
90	       cp explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh \
91	          $B/classify.py $B/microgpt-phase.sh $B/microgpt-phase.py $D/
92	       sed -i -e "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=$D|" -e "s|^LADDER_ROOT=.*|LADDER_ROOT=$D/root|" $D/run-subset.sh
93	       sed -i -e "s|/home/user/fortress|$PWD|g" \
94	           -e "s|^export LADDER_CACHES=.*|export LADDER_CACHES=$D/root/ladder-caches|" \
95	           -e "s|^export LADDER_TMP=.*|export LADDER_TMP=$D/root/ladder-tmp|" \
96	           -e "s|^RAW=.*|RAW=$D/raw/microgpt|" -e "s|^TSV=.*|TSV=$D/microgpt-results.tsv|" $D/microgpt-phase.sh
97	       tail -n +2 $B/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > $D/subset.txt
98	
99	2. Run the four scripts, with no arguments, in this order: `bash $D/run-subset.sh`, `python3 $D/classify.py`, `bash $D/microgpt-phase.sh` and `python3 $D/microgpt-phase.py`. Each reads and writes in `$D`. This takes about 200 s for the 85 and 35 s for the eighteen, so run them in the background (`session.md`, "Long commands"). #!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT="$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static"
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Step 1: the compiler-world library, in the order repo-internals.md gives.
build_library () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    local f
    for f in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do
        echo "library: $f"
        timeout 600 ../bin/fortress compile "$f" || { echo "LIBRARY BUILD FAILED on $f"; exit 1; }
    done
}

# Step 2: one known-good compiled program must print PASS before the ladder starts.
sanity () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    timeout 200 ../bin/fortress compile library_tests/Integer1.fss > /dev/null 2>&1 || return 1
    timeout 60 ../bin/fortress run Integer1 2>&1 | grep -q PASS
}

# Keep only the library's own cache entries; a program's entries are never reused.
prune_cache () {
    ( cd "$LADDER_CACHES" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.now"
    ( cd "$PRISTINE" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.keep"
    comm -23 "$LADDER_TMP/.now" "$LADDER_TMP/.keep" | while read -r p; do
        rm -f "$LADDER_CACHES/$p"
    done
}

component_of () {
    # component/api name as declared, which is what `fortress run` wants
    sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*\(component\|api\)[[:space:]]\+\([A-Za-z0-9_.]\+\).*/\2/p' "$1" | head -1
}

run_one () {
    local corpus="$1" path="$2"
    local base name comp crc rrc t0 t1 ct rt
    base=$(basename "$path")
    name="${base%.*}"
    comp=$(component_of "$path")
    [ -n "$comp" ] || comp="$name"

    t0=$(date +%s)
    timeout -k 5 "$COMPILE_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress compile "$path" \
        > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.compile" 2>&1
    crc=$?
    t1=$(date +%s); ct=$((t1-t0))

    rrc=""
    rt=""
    if [ "$crc" -eq 0 ] && [ "${base##*.}" = "fss" ]; then
        t0=$(date +%s)
        timeout -k 5 "$RUN_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress run "$comp" \
            > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.run" 2>&1
        rrc=$?
        t1=$(date +%s); rt=$((t1-t0))
    fi

    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
        "$corpus" "$base" "$comp" "$crc" "$rrc" "$ct" "$rt" >> "$TSV"
    echo "$corpus/$base crc=$crc rrc=$rrc ${ct}s"
}

main () {
    echo "=== ladder start $(date -Is) ==="
    disk_guard
    if [ ! -d "$PRISTINE" ]; then
        build_library
        rm -rf "$PRISTINE"; cp -a "$LADDER_CACHES" "$PRISTINE"
    fi
    sanity || { echo "SANITY FAILED: library_tests/Integer1 did not print PASS"; exit 1; }
    echo "sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS"
    prune_cache

    : > "$TSV"
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1

    local n=0 line corpus f
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r corpus f; do
        [ -n "$corpus" ] || continue
        run_one "$corpus" "$corpus/$f"
        n=$((n+1))
        rm -rf "${LADDER_TMP:?}"/fortress*rats
        if [ $((n % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then prune_cache; disk_guard; fi
    done < "$OUT/subset.txt"
    prune_cache
    echo "=== ladder done $(date -Is), $n files ==="
    disk_guard
}

main "$@"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored

- problem: the planner's probes, compiled on the base, die with `NoSuchMethodError` at a setter's call and at an overload method (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-35/probes/fixes-35.md:46-47`)
- spec: assigning a field calls its setter, with a right-hand side of a subtype of the field's type (`Specification/basic/expressions/bindings.tex:60-61`, `:86-87`); a functional method is a top-level function overloaded with the others, and a call runs the most specific declaration applicable at run time (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:616-626`; `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:302-311`)
- precedent: the two other sites that build an overload set before they use it split it with its subsets, `os.split(true)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7457`, `:8801`); a method's parameter type at the receiver's instance as `callTakesTupleBoxed` reads it (`CodeGen.java:7700-7726`); the cast below self's trait at a call's one argument (`CodeGen.java:8223`, `castToTypeBelow` at `:8239`)
- deviation: a call at an arrow other than the principal member's gets a second method that passes its arguments on (`forwardToPrincipal`, `CodeGen.java:8723-8755`), which no other site writes; none from the specification's spelling
- historical: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` (`CodeGen.java:7521-7527`, `:7728-7759`, `:8691-8755`)

One launch worked this rung. The worktree was seeded from the base build, `seed-worktree.sh` exit 0.

## 1. What changed and why

**Row 1053.** The desugarer turns `c.t := v` into the dotted call `c.t(v)` with no arrow (`compiler/desugarer/DesugaringVisitor.java:395-418`), and `CodeGen.forMethodInvocation` then takes the argument's static type as the call's domain (the team's own note at `CodeGen.java:7498-7503`: "some method applications (particularly those introduced during getter desugaring) don't have an OverloadingType"). The object's class declares the setter at the field's type, so where the value's type is strictly below it the call names a method the class lacks. Now a call without the checker's arrow, on a trait or object type, with an argument, takes as its domain the parameter type of the receiver type's one method of that name that has no static parameters of its own, one parameter and the return type `()`, at the receiver's instance (`setterParamType`, `CodeGen.java:7728-7759`, used at `:7521-7527`). The argument then goes through `evalArg`, whose one-argument branch casts a value of self's type below its trait (`castToTypeBelow`, `:8223`), so `s.r := self` in `trait Q comprises { R }` passes `self` cast to `R`.

**Row 815, and row 390 with it.** Where the checker leaves a call several declarations, as at the tie between a trait's functional method and that of an object that the trait's `comprises` clause lists, the overload rewrite names an overload method of those declarations, `num{...}` (`compiler/OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:112-133`), and the code generator writes it in `for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl`. That method split the set with `os.split(false)`, which never sets the set's principal member (`OverloadSet.java:419-428`), and since the team's `2fb7488717` (2012-05-09) `generateAnOverloadDefinitionInner` writes nothing without one (`OverloadSet.java:2156-2157`). So no such method was written in any component, and every call that named one died. Now the set is split with its subsets, as the two other sites do (`CodeGen.java:8707`); a name is written once, since it lists the declarations (`:8691-8694`, `:8719-8721`); and where the call's arrow is not the principal member's, a method at the call's signature passes its arguments to the set's method (`forwardToPrincipal`, `:8723-8755`). The checker breaks the tie by the overloadings' order, so `num(R)` names the method at `(R)` in one compile and at `(Q)` in another: the test program's direct compile named `FunctionalMethodComprisedObject.\=num{...}(FunctionalMethodComprisedObject$R)`, a probe of the same pair with a `Q`-typed call beside it named `(FmA$Q)`, and the one library's `Ratio` names `numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}` at `(QQ)` in one compile and at `(Ratio)` in another (section 5). Row 390's call `p(NarrowOf(1))`, beside `p(x: Wide)` and `p(x: Any)`, named the never-written `\=p{...}(fortress.AnyType$Any)` too, so it now runs; its `XXX` test turned red and is promoted (section 2).

The written method dispatches on the argument's run-time type among the set, the more specific first: for `num` it tests `instanceof R`, calls `num(R)`, and else calls `Q`'s own body (javap of the compiled test program):

    0: aload_0

    19: invokestatic  #48                 // Method "num?":(LFunctionalMethodComprisedObject$Q;)Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32;

and the method at `(R)` passes its argument on: `aload_0`, `invokestatic \=num{...}(Q)`, `areturn`.

## 2. The tests, failing on the base and passing after

Promoted: `XXXVarFieldAssignedSubtypeRun` to `compiler_tests/VarFieldAssignedSubtypeRun` (with `VarFieldAssignedSubtypeRunLink`), its program now also assigning `self` at a listed type (`trait Q comprises { R }` with `putInto(s: Slot): () = do s.r := self end`, `object Slot(var r: R)`); `XXXFunctionalMethodComprisedObject` to `FunctionalMethodComprisedObject` (with `FunctionalMethodComprisedObjectLink`); and, beyond the section, row 390's `XXXCoercionAnyOverloadRungC` to `CoercionAnyOverloadRungC` (its link test `CoercionAnyOverloadRungCLink` kept). Each run test now has `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`. `ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall` asserts `s.total` is 4321, which calls the four functional methods on `self`.

## 3. Where the fix belongs, and the precedent

The code generator (`explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md`, B.7 and the code generator's section; the brief's files). Row 1053's arrowless call comes from `DesugaringVisitor`, which both paths run (`compiler/Desugarer.java:135-138`; `fortress.compile.desugar.getset` defaults true, `Shell.java:1288`), so the call is given its domain in `CodeGen`, the compiled path's own code. Row 815's missing method is the code generator's: the checker's tie (rows 1100, 1112, 935) is a choice between two declarations that both apply, and the call's overload method is the code generator's to write.

Precedents counted: `CodeGen.java` builds an overload set at three sites; the two others split with subsets, `os.split(true)`, before using the set (`topLevelOverloadSet`, `:7457`; `generateTopLevelOverloads`, `:8801`); the third, `for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl`, split without (`:8659` on the base), and is the one that wrote nothing. - precedent: the two other sites that build an overload set before they use it split it with its subsets, `os.split(true)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7457`, `:8801`); a method's parameter type at the receiver's instance as `callTakesTupleBoxed` reads it (`CodeGen.java:7700-7726`); the cast below self's trait at a call's one argument (`CodeGen.java:8223`, `castToTypeBelow` at `:8239`)
- deviation: a call at an arrow other than the principal member's gets a second method that passes its arguments on (`forwardToPrincipal`, `CodeGen.java:8723-8755`), which no other site writes; none from the specification's spelling
- historical: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` (`CodeGen.java:7521-7527`, `:7728-7759`, `:8691-8755`)

The object's class declares the setter at the field's type, so where the value's type is strictly below it the call names a method the class lacks. Now a call without the checker's arrow, on a trait or object type, with an argument, takes as its domain the parameter type of the receiver type's one method of that name that has no static parameters of its own, one parameter and the return type `()`, at the receiver's instance (`setterParamType`, `CodeGen.java:7728-7759`, used at `:7521-7527`). The argument then goes through `evalArg`, whose one-argument branch casts a value of self's type below its trait (`castToTypeBelow`, `:8223`), so `s.r := self` in `trait Q comprises { R }` passes `self` cast to `R`.

Now the set is split with its subsets, as the two other sites do (`CodeGen.java:8707`); a name is written once, since it lists the declarations (`:8691-8694`, `:8719-8721`); and where the call's arrow is not the principal member's, a method at the call's signature passes its arguments to the set's method (`forwardToPrincipal`, `:8723-8755`). - spec: assigning a field calls its setter, with a right-hand side of a subtype of the field's type (`Specification/basic/expressions/bindings.tex:60-61`, `:86-87`); a functional method is a top-level function overloaded with the others, and a call runs the most specific declaration applicable at run time (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:616-626`; `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:302-311`)
- precedent: the two other sites that build an overload set before they use it split it with its subsets, `os.split(true)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7457`, `:8801`); a method's parameter type at the receiver's instance as `callTakesTupleBoxed` reads it (`CodeGen.java:7700-7726`); the cast below self's trait at a call's one argument (`CodeGen.java:8223`, `castToTypeBelow` at `:8239`)

## 1. What changed and why

**Row 1053.** The desugarer turns `c.t := v` into the dotted call `c.t(v)` with no arrow (`compiler/desugarer/DesugaringVisitor.java:395-418`), and `CodeGen.forMethodInvocation` then takes the argument's static type as the call's domain (the team's own note at `CodeGen.java:7498-7503`: "some method applications (particularly those introduced during getter desugaring) don't have an OverloadingType"). The object's class declares the setter at the field's type, so where the value's type is strictly below it the call names a method the class lacks. Now a call without the checker's arrow, on a trait or object type, with an argument, takes as its domain the parameter type of the receiver type's one method of that name that has no static parameters of its own, one parameter and the return type `()`, at the receiver's instance (`setterParamType`, `CodeGen.java:7728-7759`, used at `:7521-7527`). The argument then goes through `evalArg`, whose one-argument branch casts a value of self's type below its trait (`castToTypeBelow`, `:8223`), so `s.r := self` in `trait Q comprises { R }` passes `self` cast to `R`.

**Row 815, and row 390 with it.** Where the checker leaves a call several declarations, as at the tie between a trait's functional method and that of an object that the trait's `comprises` clause lists, the overload rewrite names an overload method of those declarations, `num{...}` (`compiler/OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:112-133`), and the code generator writes it in `for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl`. That method split the set with `os.split(false)`, which never sets the set's principal member (`OverloadSet.java:419-428`), and since the team's `2fb7488717` (2012-05-09) `generateAnOverloadDefinitionInner` writes nothing without one (`OverloadSet.java:2156-2157`). So no such method was written in any component, and every call that named one died. Now the set is split with its subsets, as the two other sites do (`CodeGen.java:8707`); a name is written once, since it lists the declarations (`:8691-8694`, `:8719-8721`); and where the call's arrow is not the principal member's, a method at the call's signature passes its arguments to the set's method (`forwardToPrincipal`, `:8723-8755`). The checker breaks the tie by the overloadings' order, so `num(R)` names the method at `(R)` in one compile and at `(Q)` in another: the test program's direct compile named `FunctionalMethodComprisedObject.\=num{...}(FunctionalMethodComprisedObject$R)`, a probe of the same pair with a `Q`-typed call beside it named `(FmA$Q)`, and the one library's `Ratio` names `numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}` at `(QQ)` in one compile and at `(Ratio)` in another (section 5). Row 390's call `p(NarrowOf(1))`, beside `p(x: Wide)` and `p(x: Any)`, named the never-written `\=p{...}(fortress.AnyType$Any)` too, so it now runs; its `XXX` test turned red and is promoted (section 2).

The written method dispatches on the argument's run-time type among the set, the more specific first: for `num` it tests `instanceof R`, calls `num(R)`, and else calls `Q`'s own body (javap of the compiled test program):

# Rung M of climb batch 35b: two compiled calls that the checker accepts and that die at run time (rows 1053 and 815)

- problem: the planner's probes, compiled on the base, die with `NoSuchMethodError` at a setter's call and at an overload method (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-35/probes/fixes-35.md:46-47`)
- spec: assigning a field calls its setter, with a right-hand side of a subtype of the field's type (`Specification/basic/expressions/bindings.tex:60-61`, `:86-87`); a functional method is a top-level function overloaded with the others, and a call runs the most specific declaration applicable at run time (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:616-626`; `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:302-311`)
- precedent: the two other sites that build an overload set before they use it split it with its subsets, `os.split(true)` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:7457`, `:8801`); a method's parameter type at the receiver's instance as `callTakesTupleBoxed` reads it (`CodeGen.java:7700-7726`); the cast below self's trait at a call's one argument (`CodeGen.java:8223`, `castToTypeBelow` at `:8239`)
- deviation: a call at an arrow other than the principal member's gets a second method that passes its arguments on (`forwardToPrincipal`, `CodeGen.java:8723-8755`), which no other site writes; none from the specification's spelling
- historical: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` (`CodeGen.java:7521-7527`, `:7728-7759`, `:8691-8755`)

One launch worked this rung. The worktree was seeded from the base build, `seed-worktree.sh` exit 0.

## 1. What changed and why

**Row 1053.** The desugarer turns `c.t := v` into the dotted call `c.t(v)` with no arrow (`compiler/desugarer/DesugaringVisitor.java:395-418`), and `CodeGen.forMethodInvocation` then takes the argument's static type as the call's domain (the team's own note at `CodeGen.java:7498-7503`: "some method applications (particularly those introduced during getter desugaring) don't have an OverloadingType"). The object's class declares the setter at the field's type, so where the value's type is strictly below it the call names a method the class lacks. Now a call without the checker's arrow, on a trait or object type, with an argument, takes as its domain the parameter type of the receiver type's one method of that name that has no static parameters of its own, one parameter and the return type `()`, at the receiver's instance (`setterParamType`, `CodeGen.java:7728-7759`, used at `:7521-7527`). The argument then goes through `evalArg`, whose one-argument branch casts a value of self's type below its trait (`castToTypeBelow`, `:8223`), so `s.r := self` in `trait Q comprises { R }` passes `self` cast to `R`.

**Row 815, and row 390 with it.** Where the checker leaves a call several declarations, as at the tie between a trait's functional method and that of an object that the trait's `comprises` clause lists, the overload rewrite names an overload method of those declarations, `num{...}` (`compiler/OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:112-133`), and the code generator writes it in `for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl`. That method split the set with `os.split(false)`, which never sets the set's principal member (`OverloadSet.java:419-428`), and since the team's `2fb7488717` (2012-05-09) `generateAnOverloadDefinitionInner` writes nothing without one (`OverloadSet.java:2156-2157`). So no such method was written in any component, and every call that named one died. Now the set is split with its subsets, as the two other sites do (`CodeGen.java:8707`); a name is written once, since it lists the declarations (`:8691-8694`, `:8719-8721`); and where the call's arrow is not the principal member's, a method at the call's signature passes its arguments to the set's method (`forwardToPrincipal`, `:8723-8755`). The checker breaks the tie by the overloadings' order, so `num(R)` names the method at `(R)` in one compile and at `(Q)` in another: the test program's direct compile named `FunctionalMethodComprisedObject.\=num{...}(FunctionalMethodComprisedObject$R)`, a probe of the same pair with a `Q`-typed call beside it named `(FmA$Q)`, and the one library's `Ratio` names `numerator{...}` and `denominator{...}` at `(QQ)` in one compile and at `(Ratio)` in another (section 5). Row 390's call `p(NarrowOf(1))`, beside `p(x: Wide)` and `p(x: Any)`, named the never-written `\=p{...}(fortress.AnyType$Any)` too, so it now runs; its `XXX` test turned red and is promoted (section 2).

The written method dispatches on the argument's run-time type among the set, the more specific first: for `num` it tests `instanceof R`, calls `num(R)`, and else calls `Q`'s own body (javap of the compiled test program):

    0: aload_0
    1: instanceof    #40                 // class FunctionalMethodComprisedObject$R
    11: invokestatic  #43                 // Method num:(LFunctionalMethodComprisedObject$R;)Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32;
    19: invokestatic  #48                 // Method "num?":(LFunctionalMethodComprisedObject$Q;)Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32;

and the method at `(R)` passes its argument on: `aload_0`, `invokestatic \=num{...}(Q)`, `areturn`.
